name: Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary
image_query: Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary Sikkim forest
tagline: Oak, rhododendron and red panda country an hour from Gangtok
meta_description: Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary near Gangtok: permits, timings, the Tinjure ridge walk, birding, the Golitar log house and 2026 costs.
summary: Fambong Lho is a 51 km² forest sanctuary west of Gangtok, rising from 1,524 m to 2,749 m at Tinjure. It suits birders, walkers and anyone wanting a quiet forest day close to the capital. Go from March to May or October to December, with a Forest Department permit.
intro: Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary covers about 51 km² of forested hills west of Gangtok, in Gangtok district, and touches Khangchendzonga National Park on its far side. Its slopes run from 1,524 m up to 2,749 m at Tinjure, the highest point. Streams draining it feed the Teesta and the Dikchu. Forest types change with height, from warm broadleaf woods low down to oak, rhododendron and conifers near the top, so a single day's walk passes through several of them.

This is not a safari park. There are no jeep drives and big animals are shy. What you get is a quiet, well-wooded hillside with good birding, spring flowers and the slim chance of a red panda, Sikkim's state animal. Barking deer, yellow-throated martens and Himalayan black bears live here too. Most visitors come for a day: about an hour by taxi from Gangtok to the road-head near Pangthang, then a short walk to the gate.

The sanctuary is open from 8 am to 3 pm, according to the Gangtok district administration, and you need a permit from the Forest Department with a nominal fee. Carry photo ID and two passport photos. A reserved car for the day costs about ₹2,000–3,500 from Gangtok, indicative for 2026, and a local guide is worth hiring. Rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel. Bring cash, as there are no ATMs out here.

story.title: Where two wild worlds meet above Gangtok
paras: Fambong Lho sits at a meeting point of two great zones of wildlife. Ecologists divide the world's animals into realms, and the eastern Himalaya is where the Palearctic realm of the north meets the Indomalayan realm of tropical Asia. On these slopes you find species from both. Low down, the forest is warm and broadleaf; higher up, it turns to oak, rhododendron, fir and subalpine scrub near Tinjure. The sanctuary covers about 51 km² of that gradient.

That mix is why birders come. The sanctuary's list includes hill partridge, satyr tragopan, fire-tailed myzornis, scaly laughingthrush and red-headed bullfinch, and the rufous-headed hornbill has been recorded here. Among mammals, barking deer, yellow-throated marten and red panda are reported, with musk deer and red fox at higher levels. Himalayan striped squirrels and Royle's pikas are the animals you are most likely to see. Spring, when birds call and breed, is the best time to look and listen.

The forest has also had hard times. On 4 February 2017 a large fire broke out on the Tinjure ridge, and it took several days and help from helicopters to put it out. Dry winters and strong winds raise the fire risk on these slopes, which is one reason the Forest Department controls entry. As a visitor, never light fires, never smoke on the trails, and carry out every scrap of rubbish.

did_you_know: Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary covers about 51 km² and is contiguous with Khangchendzonga National Park.
The sanctuary's highest point is Tinjure, at about 2,749 m, and its lowest parts lie at about 1,524 m.
The red panda, recorded in Fambong Lho, is the state animal of Sikkim.

highlights.title: The walk up towards Tinjure
highlights.text: The main trail climbs from the gate through oak and rhododendron forest towards Tinjure, the sanctuary's highest point at about 2,749 m. The last stretch is steep, with steps in places. On clear days the top gives views of the Kangchenjunga range. Go with a guide and start early.

highlights.title: Birding in mixed forest
highlights.text: Fambong Lho's list includes hill partridge, satyr tragopan, fire-tailed myzornis and several laughingthrushes. Early mornings from March to May are best, when birds are calling. Bring binoculars, walk slowly and keep quiet. A local bird guide improves your chances of seeing the shy species a lot.

highlights.title: Spring rhododendrons
highlights.text: From March to May, rhododendrons flower along the upper trails in reds, pinks and whites. Orchids, ferns and mosses fill the damper gullies. It is the best season for colour and for birdsong, and the weather is usually mild, with cool mornings and occasional afternoon showers.

highlights.title: A night at Golitar log house
highlights.text: The Forest Department runs a basic log house at Golitar in the buffer zone, a short walk from the Pangthang road-head. It suits walkers who want an early start and a quiet evening in the forest. Facilities are simple, and you book through the Forest Department. Check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Red panda country
highlights.text: Red pandas live in these forests, and Sikkim has made the species its state animal. Sightings are rare, as the animals are shy and spend much of their time in the canopy. Treat any glimpse as luck, not a promise, and do not pay anyone who guarantees a sighting.

how_to_reach.text: The simplest way is a reserved car from Gangtok to the road-head near Pangthang, about an hour, then a walk of roughly 20 minutes to the gate. A car with waiting time costs about ₹2,000–3,500 for the day, indicative 2026. Agree the pick-up time with your driver, as phone signal can be patchy.

There is no regular shared taxi to the sanctuary gate. Local shared taxis serve villages on the way, but timings are irregular and you may face a long walk. For a day trip with a 3 pm closing time, a reserved car or an organised trip through a registered Gangtok agent is far more practical.

Come via Gangtok. Bagdogra (IXB) is the nearest working airport and NJP the nearest big railway station, both four to five hours by road. Pakyong Airport has no scheduled flights as of 2026, and there is no railway in Sikkim yet. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Most visitors stay in Gangtok and do Fambong Lho as a day trip. Budget travellers can use the guest houses on Tibet Road and Bhanu Path, such as Hotel Sonam Delek or Mintokling Guest House, and leave by 7 am. Comfort travellers might pick Netuk House or Royal Plaza. For a night inside the forest, the Forest Department's log house at Golitar in the buffer zone is basic but well placed for an early walk; book it through the Forest Department and carry your own supplies. Some guides mention a trekkers' hut near Chuli at the top, but ask the department whether it is in use.
costs: Reserved car, Gangtok → Pangthang road-head, day return
Local nature or bird guide, day
Guided day trip with transport and lunch
budget_tip: Split one reserved car and one local guide between four people and pack lunch from Gangtok, which brings a full forest day down to well under ₹1,500 each.
tips: Get your Forest Department permit in Gangtok before the trip, with photo ID and two passport photos per person; check current status before you travel.
The sanctuary is open only from 8 am to 3 pm, so leave Gangtok by 7 am if you want time on the trail.
From June to September, leeches are common and trails slippery, so carry salt, wear long socks and consider skipping the visit.
Wear proper walking shoes and carry water, snacks and a rain layer, as there are no shops inside the sanctuary.
Never smoke or light fires: the Tinjure ridge burned for several days in February 2017, and dry winters raise the risk.

experiences.title: Guided hike towards Tinjure top
experiences.summary: A long day on foot through oak and rhododendron forest towards Tinjure, the sanctuary's highest point at about 2,749 m. The last section is steep, the views on clear days reach the Kangchenjunga range, and a local guide is essential.
body: Leave Gangtok by 7 am with your permit, packed lunch and plenty of water. The car drops you at the road-head near Pangthang, and a walk of about 20 minutes brings you to the sanctuary gate. From there the trail climbs steadily through mixed forest. Oak, rhododendron and bamboo close in overhead, and the path is often damp and mossy even in the dry season. Walk at a steady pace and take short rests.

The route towards Tinjure gains a lot of height, and the last stretch to the top is steep, with steps cut into the hillside. Allow five to seven hours for the return walk, depending on your fitness and how often you stop for birds. Because the sanctuary closes at 3 pm, turn back at an agreed time even if you have not reached the top. Your guide will know the safe turnaround point.

On a clear morning from October to December, the upper ridge gives views towards the Kangchenjunga range. In spring the reward is rhododendrons and birdsong instead. Bring a warm layer, as the top is several degrees colder than Gangtok. Do not leave the trail, do not smoke and carry out all rubbish. Walking poles help on the descent, which is hard on knees. Check current status before you travel. Expect sore legs the next day.

faqs.q: How hard is the Tinjure hike at Fambong Lho
faqs.a: It is a moderate to hard day hike. The trail climbs steadily through forest, and the last stretch to Tinjure top is steep with steps. Allow five to seven hours for the return trip. Reasonably fit walkers manage it with rests; beginners should plan to turn back partway. Go with a local guide, as trails are not well marked.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide in Fambong Lho
faqs.a: Yes, we strongly suggest one. Trails are not well signed, phone signal is patchy and the forest is home to Himalayan black bears. A local guide, about ₹800–1,500 a day, indicative for 2026, knows safe routes, turnaround times and where birds are. Ask the Forest Department or a registered Gangtok agent to arrange one with your permit.

faqs.q: Can I see Kangchenjunga from Tinjure
faqs.a: On clear mornings, yes, the upper ridge looks towards the Kangchenjunga range. Your best chance is from October to December, when the air is driest. In spring, haze and cloud often build by late morning, and from June to September the peaks are usually hidden. Start early and treat the view as a bonus.

experiences.title: Early-morning birding at Fambong Lho
experiences.summary: A slow morning on the lower trails with a local bird guide, looking for laughingthrushes, minlas, finches and, with real luck, satyr tragopan. Spring is best, when birds call and breed. Quiet walkers with binoculars do far better than groups.
body: Birding at Fambong Lho is about patience. Arrive at the gate as it opens at 8 am and walk the lower trails very slowly. Listen first, then look. Mixed flocks move through the canopy, and in spring the forest is loud with calls. Species recorded here include bar-throated and red-tailed minlas, scaly laughingthrush, black-eared shrike babbler, yellow-browed tit and crimson-browed finch. Stop often, stand still and let the birds come to you along the edges of clearings.

The birds most people hope for are harder. Satyr tragopan, a crimson pheasant with blue facial skin, lives on these forested slopes but is shy and mostly seen at dawn on quiet paths. Fire-tailed myzornis feeds on rhododendron flowers higher up. The rufous-headed hornbill has also been recorded. A good local guide knows calls and likely spots, and will not use playback recklessly, which disturbs breeding birds. Patience matters more than distance covered.

Bring binoculars, a field guide or app, a notebook and dull-coloured clothes. Walk in a small group of two to four and keep talking to a whisper. Carry tea and breakfast, as there are no stalls inside. March to May is best, with October and November a good second choice. The sanctuary closes at 3 pm. Fees and rules change, so check current status before you travel. Keep a simple list of what you see.

faqs.q: What birds can I see at Fambong Lho
faqs.a: Common finds include laughingthrushes, minlas, tits, warblers and finches. The sanctuary list also includes hill partridge, satyr tragopan, fire-tailed myzornis, red-headed bullfinch and crimson-browed finch, and the rufous-headed hornbill has been recorded. Rarer species need luck, an early start and a guide who knows their calls. March to May is the best season.

faqs.q: When is the best time for birding at Fambong Lho
faqs.a: March to May is best, when breeding birds sing and rhododendrons attract nectar feeders. October and November are a good second choice, with clearer weather and some winter visitors. Avoid June to September, when rain, leeches and mist make birding hard. Always start as early as the 8 am opening allows, as activity drops by late morning.

faqs.q: Can beginners enjoy birding at Fambong Lho
faqs.a: Yes, with a guide. A local bird guide will point out common species and help you learn calls, which makes the morning rewarding even if you miss the rarities. Carry binoculars, walk slowly and stay quiet. Beginners often enjoy the lower trails most, as they are easier underfoot and birds feed close to the path.

experiences.title: A night at the Golitar forest log house
experiences.summary: Stay a night in the Forest Department's basic log house at Golitar, in the sanctuary's buffer zone near the Pangthang road-head. You get dusk and dawn in the forest, night sounds and an early start on the trails, at a very low cost.
body: The log house at Golitar sits in the buffer zone of the sanctuary, a short walk from the road-head near Pangthang. It is run by the Forest Department, not a private hotel, so think simple: basic rooms, basic bedding and a kitchen you may need to use yourself. Book through the Forest Department in Gangtok along with your permit, and confirm what is provided before you go. Check current status before you travel.

The point of staying is time. Day visitors arrive after 8 am and leave by 3 pm, but from the log house you hear the forest at dusk and dawn. Night sounds take over after dark, and the first bird chorus starts before sunrise. In clear weather the night sky is far darker than in Gangtok. Bring a headtorch, as power can be unreliable, and a warm sleeping layer even in spring.

Carry all food from Gangtok: rice, dal, vegetables, tea, and snacks for the trail. Pack out all waste. Fires and loud music are not acceptable here. A local guide can stay nearby or meet you at dawn for the walk towards Tinjure. Rates are low, roughly ₹500–1,500 per person a night, indicative for 2026, but availability is limited, so request it well ahead. Leave the house as clean as you found it, and thank the caretaker before you go.

faqs.q: How do I book the Golitar log house
faqs.a: Book through the Sikkim Forest Department in Gangtok, ideally when you apply for your sanctuary permit. Ask what is included, such as bedding, cooking gas and utensils, and whether a caretaker will be present. Availability is limited and rules can change, so request it well in advance and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Golitar log house safe
faqs.a: It is generally safe for sensible travellers, but it is basic and remote. Do not walk the trails alone after dark, as Himalayan black bears live in the forest. Keep food sealed, carry a torch and stay with your group. Tell your hotel in Gangtok your plans, as phone signal can be patchy.

faqs.q: What should I pack for a night at Golitar
faqs.a: Pack all your food and drinking water, a headtorch, warm layers, a light sleeping bag or liner, rain gear, leech socks in the wet months, toilet paper and rubbish bags. Bring cash for the caretaker and guide, as there are no shops or ATMs nearby. Keep your permit and photo ID with you at all times.

experiences.title: Spring rhododendron walk in Fambong Lho
experiences.summary: A gentler half-day walk on the sanctuary's lower and middle trails in rhododendron season, with orchids, ferns and birdsong. It suits families and older walkers who want a real forest day without climbing to Tinjure.
body: Sikkim is famous for rhododendrons, and Fambong Lho's middle slopes are a good, uncrowded place to see them. From mid-March to early May, depending on height and the year's weather, trees flower in reds, pinks and creams. Lower down the bloom starts first; higher up it comes later. Ask your guide or the forest staff where the colour is best that week before you set off from Gangtok. Colour can vary a lot between years.

This walk does not aim for the top. Go in through the gate, follow the main trail for an hour or so, and turn back when you have had your fill. It takes three to four hours with stops. Look closer as well as up: orchids grow on mossy trunks, ferns fill the gullies, and in damp spots you will see fungi and lichens. Bring a hand lens if you like small things.

Spring weather is usually mild, but afternoon showers are common, so carry a rain jacket and leave Gangtok early. The sanctuary closes at 3 pm. Do not pick flowers or break branches; the whole sanctuary is protected and fines can apply. A reserved car costs about ₹2,000–3,500 for the day, indicative for 2026, and a local guide is worth adding even for this easier walk. Pack lunch, as there are no stalls inside.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom at Fambong Lho
faqs.a: Rhododendrons usually bloom from mid-March to early May, starting on the lower slopes and moving uphill as the season goes on. Exact timing changes each year with the weather. Late March and April usually give the most colour on the trails a day visitor can reach. Ask forest staff or your guide about the current bloom before you go.

faqs.q: Is the rhododendron walk suitable for families
faqs.a: Yes. Walking only the lower and middle trails for three to four hours is manageable for children used to walking and for fit older travellers. Paths can be uneven, damp and steep in places, so wear good shoes and go slowly. Carry snacks, water and a rain layer, as there are no shops inside.

faqs.q: Can I pick flowers in Fambong Lho
faqs.a: No. Fambong Lho is a protected wildlife sanctuary, and picking flowers, breaking branches or removing plants is not allowed. Fines can apply. Take photos instead, keep to the trail so you do not trample seedlings, and remind children before you start. Leaving the forest as you found it keeps it worth visiting.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary
faqs.a: Yes. You need a permit from the Sikkim Forest Department, with a nominal fee, indicative ₹50–200 per person in 2026. Carry photo ID and two passport photos. Foreigners also need their Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. Get the sanctuary permit in Gangtok before your trip or through a registered agent, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What are the timings of Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary
faqs.a: The sanctuary is open from 8 am to 3 pm on all days of the week, according to the Gangtok district administration. That makes early starts important: leave Gangtok by 7 am if you want a real walk. Timings can change with weather, fire risk or forest rules, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Fambong Lho from Gangtok
faqs.a: Fambong Lho lies roughly 20–30 km west of Gangtok, depending on which source and road you use. By car it takes about an hour to the road-head near Pangthang, followed by a walk of around 20 minutes to the gate. A reserved car for the day costs about ₹2,000–3,500, indicative for 2026.

faqs.q: Can I see a red panda at Fambong Lho
faqs.a: It is possible but unlikely. Red pandas live in the sanctuary, but they are shy, mostly active at dawn and dusk, and spend much time high in the trees. Most visitors never see one. Go early with a local guide, walk quietly and enjoy the birds and forest. Be wary of anyone who promises a sighting.

faqs.q: Is Fambong Lho good for a day trip from Gangtok
faqs.a: Yes. With an early start you can drive out, walk four to six hours and be back in Gangtok by evening. The 3 pm closing time is the main limit. Pack lunch, water and a rain layer, and hire a local guide. Split between four people, the car and guide cost only a few hundred rupees each.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Fambong Lho
faqs.a: March to May is best, for rhododendrons, birdsong and mild weather. October to December gives clearer skies and better mountain views from the upper trails. January and February are cold but often dry. Avoid June to September, when heavy rain, leeches, slippery trails and landslides make the visit hard and views rare.

faqs.q: Is Fambong Lho safe for trekking
faqs.a: It is reasonably safe with a local guide and sensible planning. Trails are not well marked, phone signal is patchy and Himalayan black bears live in the forest, so do not walk alone or off trail. Start early, turn back on time, and tell your hotel your plans. Avoid the monsoon months, when paths are slippery.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign nationals can visit with a valid Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, also called an Inner Line Permit, plus the Forest Department's sanctuary permit. Carry your passport, both permits and passport photos. A registered Gangtok travel agent can help with paperwork and a guide. Check current status before you travel, as rules can change.

faqs.q: Are there leeches in Fambong Lho
faqs.a: Yes, especially from June to September, when the forest is wet. Leeches are harmless but unpleasant. Wear long trousers tucked into leech socks, carry salt or a salt pouch, and check your feet and legs during breaks. From October to May they are much less of a problem, which is another reason to visit then.
